column4: The servants ask the Prophet about God, and God answers without even inserting a command to “say”; this is the clearest questioner received by nearness rather than rebuke.
The question يَسْـَٔلُونَكَ مَاذَا يُنفِقُونَ receives a revealed answer that expressly includes orphans and the needy, joining the section’s questioner and vulnerable petitioner.
The question وَيَسْـَٔلُونَكَ عَنِ ٱلْيَتَـٰمَىٰ is answered with reform and fellowship for orphans, directly meeting both the asking voice and the surah’s protected orphan.
God answers Moses’s extended petition with the compact assurance قَدْ أُوتِيتَ سُؤْلَكَ, a request met by granting rather than harshness.
Immediately after granting the request in 20:36, God begins to recount an earlier favor, so answered asking gives way to the telling of grace exactly as in the section.
The matching وَأَمَّا construction introduces the person who comes to the Prophet striving; it is the closest parallel scene to the knowledge-seeker protected in 93:10.
The approaching person of 80:8 also fears God, identifying the seriousness of the seeker whom the Prophet must receive.
The Prophet is reproved for becoming distracted from that seeker, the narrative counterpart to the command not to rebuke the asker.
Khidr tells Moses not to ask until he himself says حَتَّىٰ أُحْدِثَ لَكَ مِنْهُ ذِكْرًا; asking and the root of telling meet in one pedagogical rule.
People ask the Prophet about Dhu al-Qarnayn and he answers, سَأَتْلُوا۟ عَلَيْكُم مِّنْهُ ذِكْرًا, turning a question into an unfolding account.
The identical prohibition فَلَا تَنْهَرْهُمَا protects aged parents from a harsh voice, clarifying what the section’s تَنْهَرْ forbids toward an asker.
A kind word and forgiveness are declared better than charity followed by hurt, giving positive speech as the proper answer where material giving may wound.
When one must turn away from needy recipients, the command is still to speak قَوْلًا مَّيْسُورًا, directly protecting the petitioner from a hard refusal.
When relatives, orphans, and the needy attend a distribution, they are to receive provision and قَوْلًا مَّعْرُوفًا, pairing material care with honorable speech.
God hears the woman who pleads with the Prophet and her dialogue with him, making a socially vulnerable questioner’s voice heard and answered from above.
The righteous recognize in their wealth a due for لِّلسَّآئِلِ وَٱلْمَحْرُومِ, treating the petitioner as a rights-bearing recipient rather than an annoyance.
The known right in believers’ wealth is specified as belonging to لِّلسَّآئِلِ وَٱلْمَحْرُومِ, a direct counterpart to the person asking at the door.
God gives people from all they ask and immediately says His blessing cannot be counted, bringing request, provision, and the enumeration of favor into one ayah.
One side asks whether God’s promise proved true and the other answers نَعَمْ; the word functions at once as answer, confirmation, and recognition of a fulfilled promise.
Pharaoh’s magicians ask whether they will be rewarded if victorious, supplying the question to which 7:114 gives the section’s affirmative-answer word.
Pharaoh replies نَعَمْ and adds a promise of nearness, exactly illustrating “yes” as answer, confirmation, and promise after 7:113.
The magicians ask Pharaoh about a reward, setting up the affirmative promise in 26:42 and repeating the section’s question-and-answer structure.
The reply نَعَمْ confirms the requested reward and promises favored proximity, realizing all the answer-functions developed for the word.
The command قُلْ نَعَمْ supplies the terse affirmative answer to the resurrection questions in 37:16 and 37:17.
God calls the revelation أَحْسَنَ ٱلْحَدِيثِ, a Quranic realization of the source section’s dictionary phrase for fine or beautiful speech.
Messengers and peoples follow one another in succession and the destroyed peoples become أَحَادِيثَ, joining “one thing after another” with the stories left by events.
A confidential حَدِيث is passed on, partly disclosed, followed by the question “Who informed you?” and its answer; one speech generates another in a complete chain.
The earth will تُحَدِّثُ أَخْبَارَهَا, an explicit act of telling what happened and thus a vivid instance of the section’s command-root.
The question وَهَلْ أَتَىٰكَ حَدِيثُ مُوسَىٰ makes an interrogative voice the opening through which a narrative is told.
The question هَلْ أَتَىٰكَ حَدِيثُ ضَيْفِ إِبْرَاهِيمَ opens an account, again making inquiry the doorway to sequential telling.
The question هَلْ أَتَىٰكَ حَدِيثُ مُوسَىٰ introduces Moses’s story and repeats the section’s meeting of question and narration.
The question هَلْ أَتَىٰكَ حَدِيثُ ٱلْجُنُودِ introduces two exemplary hosts, using a question to initiate a report.
The question هَلْ أَتَىٰكَ حَدِيثُ ٱلْغَـٰشِيَةِ opens the coming scene through the very noun whose unfolding sense the section develops.
The command to remember God’s blessing then recounts enmity changed into brotherhood and rescue from a fiery brink, modeling favor told as an ordered sequence.
God commands Jesus to remember His favor to him and his mother and then enumerates its forms, an explicit divine model for recounting the Lord’s blessing.
The believers are told to remember being few and vulnerable before God sheltered, strengthened, and provided them, a striking parallel to the three successive favors in surah 93.
Joseph himself says his Lord treated him well by bringing him from prison and reuniting his family, narrating grace while assigning it to its true giver.
Moses turns أَنْعَمْتَ عَلَىَّ into a spoken pledge never to support criminals, showing remembered favor generating a new word and commitment.
Solomon answers the arrival of the throne with هَـٰذَا مِن فَضْلِ رَبِّى and names it a test of gratitude, a precise model of attributing favor to its Lord.
Whatever blessing people possess is said to be from God, stating the attribution that the phrase “your Lord’s blessing” preserves.
After God confers a favor, the person claims it was given because of his own knowledge; this directly exposes the distorted telling corrected by 93:11.
After mercy following hardship, the person says هَـٰذَا لِى, assigning the gift to himself instead of naming it as his Lord’s favor.
The people of Paradise turn to one another يَتَسَآءَلُونَ, the exact reciprocal form of asking developed in the section.
The reciprocal asking of 52:25 produces a personal account of how they formerly feared while among their families, beginning the promised unfolding speech.
The speakers then say God favored them and protected them from the Fire, turning mutual conversation into an explicit narration of divine favor.
Their account ends by recalling that they used to call upon God and by naming His goodness and mercy, completing the favor-story begun after 52:25.
The people of Paradise turn to one another يَتَسَآءَلُونَ, after which one speaker’s story emerges detail by detail.
A speaker arising from the mutual questioning in 37:50 begins, “I had a companion,” giving the first item in the ensuing sequential account.
The remembered companion’s skeptical question is quoted inside the Paradise conversation, making one dialogue generate another narrated dialogue.
A second quoted question completes the companion’s challenge about resurrection, extending the story that grew from 37:50.
The speaker asks his present companions whether they will look, moving the reciprocal exchange to its next action.
He looks and sees the former companion in the Fire, supplying the discovered consequence about which his story continues.
He addresses the companion and says he nearly brought about his ruin, interpreting the danger just shown in 37:55.
The account culminates, “Were it not for my Lord’s blessing,” explicitly assigning deliverance to the Lord within a conversation generated by mutual questioning.
A request for different foods is answered by the question whether the people would exchange what is lower for what is better, joining asking with a two-way خَيْر judgment.
“Shall I tell you of what is better than that?” combines a comparative خَيْر question with the commanded act of informing.
Those who listen to speech and follow its best are praised, connecting the section’s good speaker with discernment among spoken alternatives.
The Prophet is asked about the crescents and receives a direct answer to give, another clear instance of the questioned messenger responding through revelation.
The question about fighting in the sacred month is met with a morally differentiated answer rather than dismissal.
Two questions—about wine and gambling, then what to spend—each receive an answer in the same ayah, displaying repeated question-and-response speech.
The Prophet is asked about menstruation and is commanded to answer, preserving the questioner even around an intimate subject.
The question about what is lawful is answered with a revealed ruling, another direct يَسْـَٔلُونَكَ / قُلْ exchange.
The Prophet is asked about the Hour and commanded to state that its knowledge belongs to his Lord, an answer that also marks the limit of what he can tell.
A question about spoils receives a command to answer by assigning them to God and the Messenger and redirecting the community toward reconciliation.
The question about the spirit is answered with a bounded statement of divine command and limited human knowledge.
The Prophet is asked about the mountains and told exactly how to answer, turning inquiry into revealed description.
People ask the Prophet about the Hour and he is told to answer that its knowledge is only with God.
People ask the Prophet when the Hour will be anchored; the following ayat delimit his answer while preserving his role as warner.
People seek the Prophet’s ruling concerning women, and God answers with a ruling that expressly protects orphan girls, linking inquiry with vulnerable dependents.
People seek a ruling and God commands the Prophet to give the ruling on inheritance, a nonlexical parallel to the question-and-answer office.
Those who do not know are commanded فَسْـَٔلُوٓا۟ أَهْلَ ٱلذِّكْرِ, legitimizing the learner who approaches a knowledgeable person with a question.
The same command to ask the people of remembrance if one does not know directly dignifies inquiry as the proper response to ignorance.
The restrained poor are described as not asking people insistently, clarifying one kind of petitioner while warning that quiet need can remain unseen.
Righteous giving expressly includes وَٱلسَّآئِلِينَ, placing petitioners among concrete recipients of wealth.
Spending is kept sound only when it is not followed by reminders of generosity or injury, setting a speech boundary around aid to the needy.
Charity can be nullified by reproach and hurt, showing that a giving hand paired with an injuring voice violates the section’s ethic.
The Prophet’s divinely given gentleness keeps people near, while harshness would scatter them; this explains the human consequence of a rebuking voice.
God’s servants are commanded to say what is best because Satan creates discord between people, supplying a positive rule for the voice that replaces harsh speech.
Moses and Aaron must speak gently even to Pharaoh so he might remember or fear, an emphatic boundary against harsh address.
The covenant joins good speech to people with material care for parents, relatives, orphans, and the needy, closely matching the section’s union of voice and vulnerability.
Those managing another’s property must provide food and clothing and say قَوْلًا مَّعْرُوفًا, pairing care with fitting words.
God says He narrates أَحْسَنَ ٱلْقَصَصِ through revelation, a direct model of beautiful, unfolding narration.
The ayah asks who is better in speech than one who calls to God, does right, and openly identifies as submitted, defining excellent speech by source and effect.
A question asks whether the promised event is true and the Prophet is commanded to answer إِى وَرَبِّى, an affirmative reply explicitly grounded in his Lord.
The question “Am I not your Lord?” receives the affirmative بَلَىٰ and testimony, a Quranic affirmative form answering a negative question.
The question “Is this not the truth?” is answered بَلَىٰ, another explicit affirmative confirmation in response to an interrogative.
Moses begins the extended request answered in 20:36 by asking his Lord to expand his breast; this is the first concrete content of his سُؤْل.
He asks that his task be made easy, a second element of the petition granted as a whole in 20:36.
He asks for the knot in his tongue to be loosened, making the long petition itself partly a request for an effective voice.
The requested loosening is so people may understand his speech, stating the intended result of the voice requested in 20:27.
Moses next asks for a minister from his family, another distinct item in the request answered at 20:36.
He identifies Aaron as the brother requested for that role, specifying the person included in his petition.
Moses asks that Aaron strengthen his back, adding the requested function to the long prayer.
He asks that Aaron share his task, completing the practical request that precedes 20:36.
Moses gives abundant glorification as one purpose of the requested help, moving the petition toward the speech it is meant to enable.
He adds abundant remembrance of God, another speech-purpose embraced by the grant in 20:36.
The prayer closes by acknowledging God’s constant sight of them, immediately before the compact answer in 20:36.
The favor-story announced in 20:37 begins with revelation to Moses’s mother, the first event in the sequential telling.
God recounts the chest, river, enemy household, bestowed love, and watchful care, making several protective favors emerge one after another.
The recounting continues through his sister, restoration to his mother, rescue from killing, trial, years in Midian, and measured arrival, an extended model of narrating grace sequentially.
The frown and turning away name the adverse facial and bodily response whose correction culminates in 80:10 and parallels verbal rebuke.
The blind man’s arrival identifies the vulnerable visitor whose approach occasioned the warning continued through 80:10.
The possibility that the visitor might purify himself explains why a questioner seeking instruction cannot be dismissed by appearances.
The possibility that a reminder might benefit him states what the seeker could receive from attentive speech.
The self-sufficient person forms the social contrast to the striving seeker, exposing the status preference behind the failed reception.
The Prophet’s attention to the self-sufficient person sharpens the reversal corrected by the command concerning the asker.
The Prophet is told he is not responsible if that self-sufficient hearer does not purify himself, removing the rationale for neglecting the seeker.
After the reunion in 12:100, Joseph addresses his Lord and names the rule and interpretive knowledge given to him, continuing faithful first-person narration of gifts.
Israel is commanded to remember the blessing God bestowed, an explicit call to bring divine favor into conscious acknowledgment.
The command to remember God’s blessing is repeated with the favor of election, showing that a named blessing carries its giver with it.
A further repetition again binds remembrance of favor to God as its speaker and source.
The community must remember God’s favor and the revealed Book and wisdom by which He instructs them, linking blessing with instructive speech.
The command to remember divine favor is joined to the covenantal words “we hear and obey,” so remembered grace and a spoken response meet.
Believers are told to remember God’s favor when He restrained hostile hands, a concise example of naming a specific rescue as His gift.
Moses tells his people to remember God’s favor and then lists prophethood, kingship, and unprecedented gifts, modeling enumerated blessing in direct address.
A people are commanded to remember the favors that made them successors and increased them in stature, turning history and embodiment into named divine gifts.
Another people are commanded to remember becoming successors and being settled in the land, again attaching received conditions to their giver.
Moses tells his people to remember God’s blessing in rescue from Pharaoh’s people, an explicit prophetic retelling of favor.
Believers are commanded to remember God’s favor when armies came and unseen forces repelled them, naming deliverance as divine gift.
Humanity is commanded to remember God’s blessing and asked whether any creator besides Him provides from heaven and earth, grounding narration in the true giver.
The assertion that people cannot count God’s blessings sets a limit around the section’s exemplary enumeration: telling can name gifts without exhausting them.
David and Solomon turn knowledge into spoken praise of God who favored them, a faithful verbal attribution of an intellectual gift.
Solomon asks to be enabled to thank God for the blessing bestowed on him and his parents, making favor the content of prayerful speech.
The mature believer prays for power to thank God for blessings given to him and his parents, repeating spoken acknowledgment across generations.
Abraham praises God for granting Ishmael and Isaac in old age, a concise first-person telling of answered gift.
The condemned turn to one another يَتَسَآءَلُونَ, preserving the reciprocal-question sense in a scene whose ensuing dialogue exposes mutual blame.
The question عَمَّ يَتَسَآءَلُونَ names people asking one another, a direct occurrence of the reciprocal form developed in the prose.
“The tremendous news” identifies the subject of the reciprocal questioning in 78:1, showing mutual questions organized around a report.
This ayah poses the resurrection question to which 37:18 gives the commanded نَعَمْ, contributing the primary interrogative.
The added question about forefathers extends the challenge that the affirmative answer in 37:18 resolves.
A question, “Were we not with you?”, receives بَلَىٰ; the affirmative is genuine even though the reply then explains the fatal difference.
Guests are forbidden to linger for حَدِيث after a meal, showing the root’s ordinary social-conversation sense and the boundaries proper to it.
The Arabic Quran varies warnings so that it may يُحْدِثُ لَهُمْ ذِكْرًا, letting speech bring forth a new act of remembrance.
The possibility that God may يُحْدِثُ بَعْدَ ذَٰلِكَ أَمْرًا closely matches the dictionary image of one thing arising after another, here as a new circumstance after waiting.
The rhetorical question وَمَنْ أَصْدَقُ مِنَ ٱللَّهِ حَدِيثًا grounds trustworthy speech in God, complementing the section’s concern with rightly sourced telling.
The repeated question وَمَنْ أَصْدَقُ مِنَ ٱللَّهِ قِيلًا supplies a nonlexical parallel: divine promise is the truest speech.
Joseph asks whether scattered lords are خَيْر or the one overpowering God, a direct question seeking the better of two alternatives.
Disbelievers ask which of the two groups is خَيْر in station and assembly, illustrating a two-way “better” question distorted by worldly status.
The Prophet is commanded to ask whether that punishment is خَيْر or the promised eternal Garden, an explicit two-alternative question about the better outcome.
The commanded question ءَآللَّهُ خَيْرٌ أَمَّا يُشْرِكُونَ is the most compact Quranic instance of asking which of two is better.
The ayah asks whether the Garden’s hospitality is خَيْر or the tree of Zaqqum, another explicit binary “better” question.
The question contrasts one cast into the Fire with one who arrives secure and asks which is خَيْر, using comparison to force moral discernment.
Pharaoh asks whether he is خَيْر than Moses, showing the same comparative-question form used as arrogant self-promotion.
The question asks whether the present deniers are خَيْر or the people of Tubbaʿ, using comparison to challenge presumed security.
The question asks whether the audience’s disbelievers are خَيْر than earlier peoples, a binary comparison that denies inherited exemption.
Without using خَيْر, the ayah asks which of two walkers is better guided, a concrete nonlexical parallel to asking for the preferable of two ways.
People prefer the nearer worldly life, stating the mistaken choice that 87:17 corrects with the same better/later comparison as 93:4.
وَٱلْءَاخِرَةُ خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ directly repeats that the Hereafter is better and adds that it is more lasting.
The command to call with wisdom, good exhortation, and the best manner of argument gives concrete qualities to the constructive voice that replaces rebuke.
When the ignorant address the servants of the Merciful, they answer with peace, modeling a restrained reply even under provocation.
Moses courteously asks to follow Khidr so he can be taught, a fully staged learner’s request that leads to the speech rule in 18:70.
Khidr answers Moses’s request with a candid warning about patience rather than contempt, beginning the negotiated teacher-seeker relation.
A known right is established in the worshippers’ wealth; 70:25 then identifies the petitioner and deprived person as its recipients.
The response to the Hour-question in 79:42 challenges any assumption that the Prophet controls its final disclosure.
The endpoint of knowledge about the Hour is assigned to the Prophet’s Lord, defining the truthful limit of his answer.
The Prophet’s own role is restricted to warning the one who fears it, clarifying the stance from which he answers 79:42.
The community is warned against asking its Messenger as Moses was culpably asked before, a boundary showing that protecting an asker does not endorse every demand.
The People of the Book demand a book from heaven and are recalled as having asked Moses for something still greater, exemplifying coercive questioning rather than teachable inquiry.
Believers are told not to ask questions whose disclosed answers would distress them, marking a substantive limit on questioning without licensing harsh treatment of people.
Earlier people asked such questions and then rejected their answers, supplying the failure that explains the warning in 5:101.
Noah is told not to ask God for what he lacks knowledge of, a boundary on the petitioner’s claim grounded in truth rather than social status.
Moses himself accepts that another question will end his companionship with Khidr, a negotiated pedagogical boundary after repeated breaches.
At the trumpet blast people لَا يَتَسَآءَلُونَ, a direct negation of reciprocal questioning when ordinary relationships collapse.
On the Day of Judgment answers become obscure and people do not ask one another, reversing the section’s living exchange of question and response.
God is not questioned about what He does while people will be questioned, marking the ultimate asymmetry within the root’s otherwise reciprocal possibilities.
People recognize God’s blessing and then deny it, the opposite of telling the favor while faithfully naming its source.
Those who exchange God’s blessing for unbelief transform received favor into ruin, a reversal of grateful narration.
Pharaoh cites his upbringing of Moses as a “favor” used to reproach and control him; Moses exposes how telling a benefit can itself become injurious speech.
Qarun claims his wealth was given because of knowledge he possesses, the same self-crediting distortion that the section opposes.
The garden owner boasts that he is greater in wealth and followers, supplying the self-magnifying speech corrected by 18:39.
He enters his garden wronging himself and claims it will never perish, treating the gift as self-secured rather than entrusted.
He speculates that even if returned to his Lord he will find something خَيْر, misusing “better” to extend entitlement into the Hereafter.
His companion supplies the missing speech, مَا شَآءَ ٱللَّهُ لَا قُوَّةَ إِلَّا بِٱللَّهِ, teaching how the garden should have been verbally attributed.
A person interprets expanded provision by saying “My Lord has honored me,” showing that even naming the Lord can misread what a favor means.
When provision is restricted, the same person says “My Lord has humiliated me,” and the next ayah’s rejection marks this speech as a false measure of divine regard.
When told to spend from God’s provision, disbelievers answer with a contemptuous refusal to feed the needy, staging the harsh voice opposite the section’s command.
Every newly arriving reminder is heard while people play, showing speech that produces no attentive “thing after thing” because its hearers trivialize it.
Each renewed reminder from the Merciful is met by turning away, the reception opposite both listening to a questioner and responding to a divine account.
Jacob says God will teach Joseph the interpretation of ٱلْأَحَادِيثِ and complete His blessing upon him and his family, bringing the roots of narration and favor together in one promise.
Immediately after the people of Paradise narrate favor in 52:25–28, the Prophet is commanded to remind, and his freedom from soothsaying or madness is attributed to بِنِعْمَتِ رَبِّكَ.
The divine voice says the Prophet is not mad بِنِعْمَةِ رَبِّكَ, repeating the section’s exact attribution of blessing to his Lord.
The question “Have We not expanded your breast?” addresses the Prophet with the first item in another ordered divine recounting of favors.
God names removal of the Prophet’s burden as the second favor in the sequence begun at 94:1.
The burden is identified by what weighed on his back, giving concrete force to the relief narrated in 94:2.
God adds the raising of the Prophet’s remembrance, completing a compact succession of favors comparable to 93:6–8.
The Prophet is forbidden to drive away humble people who call on their Lord, directly protecting low-status seekers from exclusion.
The Prophet must remain patiently with those who call on their Lord and must not look past them toward worldly adornment, closely paralleling the status reversal in the seeker scene.
Noah says he asks no wealth, assigns his reward to God, and refuses to drive believers away, joining non-demanding prophetic speech with protection of socially dismissed hearers.
Noah states that he will not drive believers away, a direct nonlexical counterpart to receiving the vulnerable person without rebuke.
Everyone in the heavens and earth asks God while He is each day bringing about a matter, joining universal petition with continuing divine response.
God commands people to call upon Him and promises to answer, presenting the petitioner as invited and the response as assured.
God asks Abraham whether he does not believe; Abraham answers بَلَىٰ and explains his request for reassurance, combining an affirmative reply with a petitioner whose further question is received.
The keepers ask each arriving group whether no warner came, supplying the question answered affirmatively and then narrated in 67:9.
The condemned answer بَلَىٰ and proceed to recount the warner’s coming and their denial, so an affirmative answer generates a sequential report.
Their account concludes that listening or reasoning would have averted their fate, stating the consequence of refusing the warning described in 67:9.
God tells the Prophet that messenger accounts are narrated to steady his heart and bring truth, admonition, and reminder, explaining what sequential telling produces.
God says He recounts reports of what preceded and has given the Prophet a reminder, another direct divine description of narrative address.
The Prophet is commanded to recite truthfully the report of Adam’s two sons, a direct counterpart to the command to tell.
The Prophet is commanded to recite a person’s report so that hearers may reflect, explicitly assigning a purpose to narration.
The Prophet is commanded to recite Noah’s report, another repeated formulation of divinely ordered telling.
The Prophet is commanded to inform people about Abraham’s guests, after which their encounter unfolds in successive speech.
The Prophet is commanded to recite Abraham’s report, repeating the stance of a divinely instructed narrator.
After disbelievers deny that the Hour will come, the Prophet is commanded to answer بَلَىٰ وَرَبِّى, an affirmation grounded in his Lord and followed by a promise.
After denial of resurrection, the Prophet is commanded to say بَلَىٰ وَرَبِّى and affirm both resurrection and disclosure of deeds.
When the condemned are asked whether the encounter is true, they answer بَلَىٰ وَرَبِّنَا, an affirmative response that explicitly names their Lord.
Abraham begins an ordered first-person account: the Lord who created him is the one who guides him.
Abraham next names God as the one who feeds him and gives him drink, continuing the narrated benefits.
He next attributes healing during illness to God, adding another concrete favor to the sequence.
He then names death and restored life as God’s acts, extending the account beyond present provision.
The sequence culminates in Abraham’s hope that his Lord will forgive his fault on Judgment Day.
The people of Paradise praise God for guiding them and say they could not have been guided without Him, a faithful spoken attribution of saving favor.
Noah is instructed to praise God after being delivered from wrongdoers, turning rescue into an explicit spoken acknowledgment.
The people of Paradise praise God who removed sorrow from them, narrating their changed condition while naming its giver.
The inheritors of Paradise praise God for fulfilling His promise and granting them the land, combining fulfilled promise, gift, and verbal acknowledgment.
The recipients of the surah’s favors are commanded to worship the Lord of the House, directing their response to the giver named in 106:4.
The Lord is identified as the one who fed them against hunger and secured them against fear, a paired recounting of provision and shelter.
God directly tells the Prophet that He has given him abundance, a concise divine narration of favor.
Prayer and sacrifice are commanded as the response to the gift stated in 108:1, showing favor generating a new act and voice.
Solomon says what God has given him is better than the envoys’ gift, combining correct divine attribution with a خَيْر comparison.
The addressee is told to ask one who is informed about the Merciful, another explicit validation of inquiry directed to knowledge.
Instead of coveting unequal allotments, people are commanded to ask God for His bounty, redirecting petition toward the giver.
Joseph and his brothers are said to contain signs for ٱلسَّآئِلِينَ, treating questioners as people to whom a narrated story yields knowledge.
Sacrificial meat is to feed both the contented person and the one who asks, a material answer to distinct forms of need.
God promises reward without asking believers for their wealth; 47:37 then explains the human response if such asking were pressed.
If God were to ask people for wealth and press them, they would become stingy and their resentments would emerge, exposing the social tension around importunate request.
Joseph’s establishment in the land is linked to being taught the interpretation of ٱلْأَحَادِيثِ, extending the root from spoken reports to meaningful dreams or events.
The Prophet must leave mockers of revelation until they enter a different حَدِيث, showing that conversation has moral boundaries and can be replaced by another.
Idle or misleading لَهْوَ ٱلْحَدِيثِ is purchased to divert people from God’s way, a specific reversal of speech that gives rise to guidance.
After the false claim in 41:50, favor makes the person turn away while harm produces prolonged supplication, exposing the distorted relation between gift and voice.
When favored, the human turns aside; when touched by evil, he despairs, the opposite of receiving favor and then speaking grateful acknowledgment.
A distressed person calls on his Lord, but after receiving a blessing forgets the earlier prayer and assigns rivals to God.
A tasted mercy produces self-satisfaction, while adversity exposes human ingratitude, another specific reversal of the response appropriate to favor.
People enjoy a secure sanctuary yet believe falsehood and deny God’s blessing, suppressing the gift’s true attribution.
God’s proclamation promises increase for gratitude and warns of punishment for ingratitude, stating what follows from the response to favor.
Jonah’s escape from being cast blameworthy is attributed to a blessing from his Lord, another narrated rescue with its giver named.
The rescue of Lot’s household is called a favor from God and a recompense for gratitude, linking delivered grace to thankful response.
